title: Novel Resistance Training-Specific Rating of Perceived Exertion Scale Measuring Repetitions in Reserve
authors: Zourdos MC, Klemp A, Dolan C, Quiles JM, Schau KA, Jo E, Helms E, Esgro B, Duncan S, Garcia Merino S, Blanco R
journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
population: 29 adults (mean age 24.0 years) who squatted: 15 experienced squatters (training age 5.2 +/- 3.5 years) and 14 novice squatters (0.4 +/- 0.6 years). Not runners.
findings: Each person performed a 1RM squat, then one repetition at 60, 75 and 90% of 1RM and an 8-repetition set at 70% 1RM, and rated each with an effort score that matched repetitions in reserve (RPE 10 = 0 reps in reserve, RPE 9 = 1 in reserve, and so on).

Average barbell velocity was slower in the experienced than in the novice squatters at 100% and 90% 1RM (p <= 0.05) and did not differ at 60 and 75% 1RM or on the first and eighth repetitions of the 70% set (p > 0.05). The experienced group rated the 1RM as harder (p = 0.023).
Average velocity and the effort score were strongly inversely related at all intensities, r = -0.88 in the experienced and r = -0.77 in the novice squatters.
The authors call the reps-in-reserve effort scale a practical method to regulate daily training load and to give feedback during a 1RM test.
limitations: One lift (the barbell squat) in 29 young adults, mostly at single repetitions and one set of 8; it relates the effort rating to bar velocity and does not test whether a load prescribed by reps in reserve gives better strength or running results than another method. No runners, no women-only or older group stated in the abstract. Abstract read; full text not read.
implications: Supports using a count of repetitions in reserve as a daily effort target for a squat, with a measurable link to bar speed in novice and experienced lifters. It does not validate the target values the engine uses (f7.heavyRir, f7.easyRir), which stay grade D.
The rating was checked against velocity, not against the true number of repetitions left; the accuracy of that count is the subject of the Halperin 2021 review.
